blocks.text: India has a **single, integrated judiciary** enforcing both Union and state laws — unlike the American dual system. The pyramid: **Supreme Court (Arts 124–147)** → **High Courts (Arts 214–231)** → **subordinate courts (Arts 233–237)**: district & sessions judges, and below them civil judges and judicial magistrates. **Andhra Pradesh High Court** sits at **Amaravati (Nelapadu)** since 1 January 2019, carved from the common Hyderabad High Court under the **Reorganisation Act**.

rows: President, via the **collegium** (CJI + 4 seniormost) — Second & Third Judges cases (1993, 1998); **NJAC struck down (2015)** for violating judicial independence
Collegium of CJI + 2, consulting HC & Governor
Till **65**; removal by special-majority address for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity** (Art 124(4), Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968)
Salaries charged on CFI; conduct not discussable (Art 121); contempt power (Art 129); ban on post-retirement practice (Art 124(7))
Analogous (Arts 215, 220 — practice barred except SC/other HCs)

items: **Original**: **Art 131** — Centre–state and inter-state disputes (AP invoked it against neighbouring states in river matters); **Art 32** — writs for fundamental rights ('the very soul of the Constitution' — Ambedkar).
**Appellate**: constitutional (Art 132), civil (133), criminal (134), and **special leave (Art 136)** — the widest discretionary appellate power in any constitution.
**Advisory**: **Art 143** — Presidential references (e.g., Berubari 1960, Keshav Singh 1965, the 2025 reference on Governors' timelines).
**Review & curative**: Art 137; **Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002)** created the curative petition.
**High Courts**: writs under **Art 226 (wider than Art 32 — 'any other purpose')**, superintendence over all courts/tribunals (**Art 227**), and control over subordinate judiciary (Art 235).

**Subordinate courts + system reforms**: All-India Judicial Service debate (Art 312 permits), **Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008**, Lok Adalats (Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 — **Art 39A** legal aid), fast-track and commercial courts, e-Courts Phase III.

items: **Pendency ~5 crore cases**; vacancy rates of 20–30% in HCs; judge-population ratio (~21 per million) far below the Law Commission's 50 (120th Report).
**Collegium opacity vs executive delay**: names reiterated but not notified; the **Memorandum of Procedure** remains unsettled since NJAC (2015).
**Undertrial burden** (~75% of prisoners) — bail reform urged in **Satender Kumar Antil (2022)**.

**Tribunalisation** and its discontents — **Chandra Kumar (1997)**: tribunal decisions face HC review; repeated SC strictures on tribunal vacancies (incl. the **AP Administrative Tribunal** framework under Art 371D).
**Reform basket**: NJIC/judicial infrastructure authority, AIJS, transparent collegium criteria, case-flow management, ODR/e-Courts, regional benches debate (Art 130).

blocks.text: Exam tip: 'Structure and functions of the judiciary' invites a diagram-led answer: pyramid + jurisdiction table + three reform points with data (pendency, vacancies, undertrials). Add the AP High Court at Amaravati and the Art 371D tribunal as state colour.

sections.heading: 🏛 Deep mastery — collegium, pendency and reform

items: **The appointments debate:** the **Collegium system** emerged from the **Three Judges Cases** (1981 First, 1993 Second, 1998 Third); the **99th Amendment & NJAC Act** were struck down in *SC Advocates-on-Record Association* (2015) as violating judicial independence (basic structure). The **Memorandum of Procedure** friction between Executive and Collegium persists.

**Pendency crisis:** over **5 crore cases** pending across courts (NJDG data); causes — judge vacancies (sanctioned strength unfilled), adjournments, low judge-to-population ratio (~21 per million vs the Law Commission's recommended 50).

**Reform toolkit:** All India Judicial Service (Art 312 allows it), fast-track & commercial courts, **Lok Adalats & Gram Nyayalayas**, plea bargaining, ADR (Arbitration & Mediation Act 2023), and e-Courts Phase III for digitisation.

blocks.text: **AP angle:** the **AP High Court at Amaravati** (bifurcated from the common Hyderabad HC in 2019) and the **AP State Legal Services Authority** (NALSA architecture) anchor access-to-justice answers; **Lok Adalats** clear lakhs of cases in the state.

prelimsPointers: **NJAC (99th Amendment)** struck down in 2015; **Collegium** restored.
**AP High Court** established at **Amaravati** on 1 January 2019 after bifurcation of the common High Court.
SC strength is fixed by **Parliament by law** — currently **34 including the CJI** (2019 amendment).
**Art 32 is itself a fundamental right**; suspension possible only via Art 359 during Emergency.
**Art 226 is wider than Art 32** — writs for fundamental rights *and* 'any other purpose'; Art 226 is not suspended by an emergency proclamation as such.
A common High Court for two or more states is possible under **Art 231** (AP & Telangana shared one during 2014–18; separate AP HC from 1 Jan 2019).
**NJAC (99th Amendment)** struck down in the **Fourth Judges case (2015)** — judicial primacy in appointments is basic structure.
District judges are appointed by the **Governor in consultation with the High Court (Art 233)**.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**: judicial review under Arts 32/226 is basic structure; tribunal orders appealable to HC Division Bench.
mainsAngles: 'Justice delayed is the Indian judiciary's deepest legitimacy crisis' — analyse causes of pendency and evaluate structural remedies.
The collegium system survives because every alternative has looked worse — critically examine post-NJAC options for appointment reform.
Discuss the constitutional scheme for judicial independence and whether post-retirement appointments undermine it.
Assess the promise and performance of the subordinate-judiciary reforms: Gram Nyayalayas, Lok Adalats and e-Courts.

glossary.definition: Judge-led appointment mechanism (CJI + seniormost colleagues) evolved through the Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges cases; constitutionally entrenched by the NJAC verdict (2015).
Art 136 discretionary power of the Supreme Court to hear appeal against any order of any court or tribunal — the widest appellate gate in the system.
Post-review remedy created in Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002) to cure gross miscarriage of justice, heard by the three seniormost judges plus the bench concerned.
Court whose records have evidentiary value and which can punish for its contempt — the SC (Art 129) and HCs (Art 215).
Proposed centralised recruitment for district judges under Art 312 — requires a Rajya Sabha resolution; debated as a cure for vacancies and diversity deficits.

blocks.text: **Part XVIII (Arts 352–360)** lets the Union temporarily convert the federal system into a unitary one. The **44th Amendment (1978)** — the corrective to the 1975–77 Emergency — rebuilt every safeguard: 'internal disturbance' became **'armed rebellion'**, written Cabinet advice was made mandatory, and approval/renewal rules were tightened.

rows: War, external aggression, **armed rebellion**; written recommendation of the **Cabinet**
Both Houses within **1 month** by **special majority**; 6 months at a time, indefinitely renewable; LS may revoke by simple majority (1/10 members can requisition)
Union directs states; Parliament legislates on State List; **Art 358** suspends Art 19 (only for war/external aggression); **Art 359** suspends enforcement of FRs **except Arts 20–21**
Failure of constitutional machinery (report of Governor or otherwise); **Art 365** non-compliance
Both Houses within **2 months** (simple majority); 6 months at a time; max **3 years** (beyond 1 year only with Emergency in force + EC certification — 44th Amdt)
President assumes executive; Parliament/delegate legislates; **Assembly suspended or dissolved — judicial review per Bommai**
Threat to financial stability or credit
Both Houses within 2 months; **continues indefinitely once approved**
Salary reductions incl. judges; money bills reservable; **never invoked**

blocks.text: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** domesticated Art 356: proclamations are judicially reviewable, majority is tested on the **floor of the House**, the Assembly cannot be dissolved before parliamentary approval, and mala fide use invites restoration of the government. Use of Art 356 has fallen sharply since — the judgment is the textbook example of judicial review disciplining a political power.

rows: New states (Arts 3–4, AP Reorganisation Act 2014), citizenship, salaries, Second Schedule
Majority of total membership **+ 2/3 present & voting**, each House separately (no joint sitting)
Special majority **+ ratification by half the states**
As above + simple-majority resolutions of ≥ half the state legislatures
Election of President, Union–state relations, Seventh Schedule, representation of states, Art 368 itself, SC/HC provisions — e.g., **GST (101st)**

items: **Shankari Prasad (1951)** & **Sajjan Singh (1965)**: amendments are not 'law' under Art 13 — FRs amendable.
**Golak Nath (1967)**: FRs unamendable → Parliament answered with the **24th Amendment (1971)**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges)**: Parliament may amend anything but not the **basic structure**.

**Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975)** & **Minerva Mills (1980)**: struck clauses (39th & 42nd Amdt) exalting amending power; **limited amending power is itself basic structure**; balance of FRs–DPSPs protected.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: Ninth Schedule insertions after 24-4-1973 are reviewable — confirmed in **I.R. Coelho (2007)**.

  F --> G{Violates basic structure?}
  G --> H[Struck down - Kesavananda 1973]
  G --> I[Valid]

items: Emergency architecture post-44th Amendment is a study in **learning from abuse**: compare 1975 (Art 359 suspending Art 21, **ADM Jabalpur** — formally overruled in **Puttaswamy, 2017**) with today's non-derogable Arts 20–21.
Amendment procedure shows the **blend of rigidity and flexibility** — and the basic-structure doctrine adds an unwritten rigidity that has kept the Constitution supreme for five decades.

**AP hooks**: composite AP saw President's Rule (notably 2014, just before bifurcation); the **32nd Amendment (Art 371D)** and the **101st (GST)** both illustrate amendment routes; the state's creation and bifurcation used the **simple-majority Art 3–4 route**, not Art 368.

blocks.text: Exam tip: For emergencies, the 44th-Amendment safeguards ARE the answer skeleton. For amendments, the six-case doctrinal ladder (Shankari Prasad → Coelho) with years is non-negotiable; close with 'flexible enough to grow, rigid enough to endure'.

sections.heading: 🏛 Deep mastery — emergencies after the 44th Amendment

blocks.text: The **44th Amendment (1978)**, a direct response to the 1975–77 Emergency, rebuilt safeguards: 'internal disturbance' was replaced by **'armed rebellion'** (Art 352); proclamation needs **written Cabinet advice**; parliamentary approval within **one month** by special majority, renewable every **six months**; **Arts 20 & 21 can never be suspended**; and the right to property was removed from Fundamental Rights (**Art 300A**, a legal right).

rows: Cabinet's written advice; approval in 1 month; judicially reviewable (*Minerva Mills*)
*S.R. Bommai* (1994): floor test, reviewable, federalism is basic structure

blocks.text: **ADM Jabalpur (1976)** — which suspended habeas corpus — was **expressly overruled in *K.S. Puttaswamy* (2017)**; Art 21 stands even in emergency. This is the redemption arc examiners love.

prelimsPointers: **44th Amendment (1978)** — 'armed rebellion' replaces 'internal disturbance'; Arts 20 & 21 non-suspendable.
**ADM Jabalpur (1976)** overruled by **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
National Emergency has been proclaimed **thrice**: 1962 (China), 1971 (Pakistan), 1975 ('internal disturbance').
**Art 358** operates only for **war/external aggression**, automatically, and only against **Art 19**; **Art 359** needs a Presidential order and can never bar **Arts 20–21** (44th Amdt).
President's Rule approval: **simple majority within 2 months**; beyond one year needs Emergency + ECI certification.
**Financial Emergency (Art 360)** has **never been proclaimed**; once approved it continues indefinitely.
Amendment bills: introduced in **either House**, no prior Presidential recommendation, **no joint sitting**; President **must assent** (24th Amdt).
State ratification needs **half the states by simple majority**; no time limit prescribed.
**ADM Jabalpur (1976)** expressly overruled in **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)**.
mainsAngles: 'The 44th Amendment converted the Emergency provisions from a sword into a shield' — examine.
S.R. Bommai is the finest example of judicial review revitalising federalism — discuss the decline of Article 356 since 1994.
Trace the evolution of the basic structure doctrine and assess whether it is counter-majoritarian or democracy-protecting.
Compare the procedure under Article 368 with the simple-majority route of Articles 3–4, using the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.

glossary.definition: Ground substituted for 'internal disturbance' in Art 352 by the 44th Amendment (1978), raising the threshold for a National Emergency.
Deeming provision: a state's failure to comply with Union directions permits the President to hold that constitutional machinery has failed — the bridge to Art 356.

Core features of the Constitution (supremacy, republican democracy, secularism, federalism, judicial review, FR–DPSP balance) that even a valid Art 368 amendment cannot abrogate — Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
Technique first used in Golak Nath (1967): a new ruling applies only prospectively, saving past transactions.
Schedule (1st Amendment, Art 31B) immunising listed laws from FR challenge; post-24 April 1973 insertions are reviewable on basic-structure grounds (I.R. Coelho, 2007).

blocks.text: Judicial review is the power of constitutional courts to **examine the validity of legislative and executive action** and strike down what offends the Constitution. Unlike the USA (where *Marbury v. Madison* implied it), India's text is explicit: **Art 13** (laws inconsistent with FRs are void), **Arts 32/226** (writs), **Arts 131–136** (appellate/original), **Art 245** (competence), plus **Arts 251, 254, 372**. **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** declared review under Arts 32/226 part of the **basic structure**.

rows: Competence (lists), FR violation, basic structure (for amendments)
**E.P. Royappa (1974); Maneka Gandhi (1978)** — fair, just, reasonable procedure

blocks.text: Scorecard of review in action: striking **Sec 66A IT Act (Shreya Singhal, 2015)**, **electoral bonds scheme (ADR v. Union, Feb 2024)** for violating voters' right to information, decriminalising **Sec 377 (Navtej, 2018)** and **adultery (Joseph Shine, 2018)** — alongside deference phases that critics call 'judicial evasion'.

PIL relaxed **locus standi**: any public-spirited person may move the court for those unable to reach it. Architects: **Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati** (late 1970s–80s). Milestones: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)** — speedy trial for undertrials; **S.P. Gupta (1981)** — the doctrinal charter ('judges case'); **Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984)** — bonded labour; **M.C. Mehta** series — environmental law (absolute liability, **Art 21** right to clean environment); **Vishaka (1997)** — workplace sexual-harassment guidelines (now the 2013 Act); **Ganga/forest continuing mandamus** cases.

  B --> C[Court relaxes locus standi - PIL admitted]

items: **Achievements**: converted Art 21 into a rights-cornucopia (food — **PUCL 2001** interim orders birthing NFSA; shelter; health; clean air), disciplined custodial violence (**D.K. Basu, 1997**), forced electoral transparency (**ADR 2002** — candidate disclosures).
**Pathologies**: 'publicity-interest litigation', forum shopping, policy overreach (judicially-run sports bodies, liquor-highway rules), and the separation-of-powers objection.
**Filters now applied**: **Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010)** guidelines — verify credentials, screen motives, impose exemplary costs on frivolous petitions.

sections.heading: Activism vs restraint — and the AP thread

items: The line runs: **review is legitimacy** (courts enforcing the Constitution) but **governance is not adjudication** — 'the court must not become the first resort for what are essentially political questions'. The doctrine of **separation of powers is itself basic structure (Indira Nehru Gandhi, 1975)** — cutting both ways.

**AP thread**: PILs and review have shaped AP's public life — the AP High Court's scrutiny of local-body election scheduling (2020–21), Godavari/Krishna environmental compliance petitions, Amaravati-capital litigation (the **three-capitals** matter, where the HC in 2022 mandated capital development and the appeal is pending in the SC) — a live example of courts adjudicating high policy.
Balanced conclusion: PIL is 'the Indian judiciary's most original contribution to constitutionalism'; its credibility depends on **self-restraint plus rigorous filters**.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Define review → constitutional anchors (Arts 13/32/226) → basic-structure status (Chandra Kumar) → PIL genesis, three achievement cases, two pathology points, Chaufal filters → one AP example (three-capitals litigation). That sequence answers every phrasing of this question.

sections.heading: 🏛 Deep mastery — PIL, review and the activism debate today

items: **Judicial review's textual base:** Arts **13, 32, 226, 227, 245–246**; strengthened by *Kesavananda* (review is basic structure) and *Puttaswamy* (privacy as Art 21).

**PIL milestones:** *Hussainara Khatoon* (speedy trial), *S.P. Gupta* (locus standi widened), *M.C. Mehta* (environmental jurisprudence, absolute liability), *Vishaka* (workplace sexual harassment guidelines) — judge-made law filling legislative gaps.

**The activism–restraint balance:** critics cite 'judicial overreach' (courts entering policy — e.g., liquor-highway ban, cracker bans); defenders cite executive/legislative abdication. **Continuing mandamus** and expert committees are the modern via media.
**Overreach vs accountability:** debates on judicial vacancies, the collegium's opacity, and the demand for judicial accountability (post-*C. Ravichandran Iyer*) frame the reform conversation.

mainsAngles: 'Public Interest Litigation democratised justice but risks judicial adventurism' — critically examine.
Where should the line be drawn between judicial review and judicial overreach? Illustrate with recent cases.

prelimsPointers: **Art 13(2)**: the State shall not make any law abridging FRs; 'law' includes ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules and custom — but NOT constitutional amendments (per 24th Amdt, subject to basic structure).
Writs: **habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto** — Art 32 (FRs only) vs Art 226 (any purpose).
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**: Arts 32/226 review is basic structure; tribunals subordinate to HC review.
PIL pioneers: **Justices P.N. Bhagwati & V.R. Krishna Iyer**; first major PILs — Hussainara Khatoon (1979), S.P. Gupta (1981).
**Vishaka (1997)** guidelines drew on **CEDAW**; replaced by the Sexual Harassment Act, 2013.
**Shreya Singhal (2015)** struck **Sec 66A IT Act**; **ADR (2024)** struck the electoral bonds scheme.
PIL filters: **State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010)**.
mainsAngles: 'Judicial review is the balance wheel of the Constitution' — examine its constitutional foundations and outer limits.
PIL democratised access to justice but risks judicial populism — critically evaluate with milestones and correctives.
Is the basic-structure doctrine judicial supremacy or constitutional self-defence? Argue with Kesavananda, Minerva Mills and the NJAC case.
Courts increasingly decide questions of pure governance — assess with reference to Andhra Pradesh's capital litigation and the doctrine of separation of powers.
Proportionality has replaced Wednesbury as the pole star of rights review — discuss post-Puttaswamy.

glossary.definition: The requirement that only an aggrieved person may sue; its relaxation for public causes is the doctrinal foundation of PIL.
Court keeping a case open and issuing rolling directions with compliance monitoring — used in environmental and investigation-supervision PILs.
Ground of review where a decision is so irrational that no reasonable authority could reach it; increasingly supplemented by structured proportionality.
Four-stage test (legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, balancing) for reviewing rights restrictions — canonised in Puttaswamy (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin (2020).
Treating letters or postcards from victims or activists as writ petitions — the access innovation of early PIL.
Court action crossing from interpreting law into policy-making or administration — the standing critique of expansive PIL.
